speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most honoured to join the ranks of the many who, in the past, have debated a motion to increase the old age security pension and to lower the age of eligibility. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has, with this motion, again demonstrated his unswerving dedication to older Canadians.
I support his motives, as I believe do all hon. members in this House. Let me say that as an actuary I have long been concerned by the inadequacies in our pension systems, both public and private. Let me also say that my government cares about senior citizens. We would like the retirement of every Canadian to be totally secure and fulfilled. We have, over the years, pressed for and supported changes and improvements in our social programs that would help reach that goal.
The most recent evidence, as the hon. member indicated, of this government's commitment to older Canadians was the introduction, on October 17, of a bill to amend the spouse's allowance provisions of the Old Age Security Act. If approved, this bill will allow us to amend what was one of the most poorly designed pieces of legislation ever to be introduced into the House. We condemn the practice of creating false expectations, of giving a spouse's allowance to an OAS pensioner's spouse, and then withdrawing it arbitrarily with wanton disregard for that spouse's emotional state and financial circumstances.
I spoke a moment ago of the quality of retirement that we would like to see for older Canadians. By "we" I do not mean we, the government, nor we, the members of this House. I mean we as Canadians-government and citizens. It is together that we must strive to realize our objective.
In looking today at these proposed changes to the Canada Pension Plan and the old age security program, I am reminded of misconceptions that often give rise, or at least relate, to suggestions such as those contained in this motion. I would not suggest that there was any such misconception on the part of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he formulated these proposals, but I do think it might shed some light on this debate if we looked at these for a moment.
[ Translation]
The first concept to which I refer is that the problems of senior citizens can be solved by merely increasing the basic old age security pension. Without mentioning the cost of implementing the formula, I consider this as a rigid perception of the issue: all pensioners need the same retirement income and

the state assumes all responsibilities. I urge hon. members and all Canadians, particularly older citizens, to examine carefully and seriously with me what the implementation of such a measure would cost. The hon. member would like to raise to $350 the basic old age security benefits, but he does not ask himself if Canadian taxpayers are prepared to pay almost twice the cost of the existing old age security program, which means annual expenditures exceeding $9 billion. This amount does not include the huge cost of benefits paid because the eligibility age will have been lowered and the means test abolished, as is also recommended in the proposal of the hon. member. Those $9 billion will have to be paid not just for one year but year after year and this amount will continuously increase. I do not believe that our economy or the Canadian taxpayer have the financial means to pay for it, or that senior citizens wish to impose such a heavy burden on their children and grandchildren. In fact, everyone has different retirement needs. It depends to a large extent on the income level you had during your active life and on your standard of living. This is why the retirement system in Canada has undergone the changes we have seen.
The government, rather than merely implementing a single program to meet all the income needs of retired people, preferred to develop a three-fold formula. This formula recognizes both public and individual responsibilities concerning retirement and faithfully reflects, I think, the values and attitudes of Canadians on that matter.

But let me once again stress that it would be completely irresponsible to increase our deficit by over $4 billion at a time when our deficit exceeds $10 billion. Day after day we hear from hon. members opposite about their concern over the fact that interest rates are too high. Increases of this magnitude in government spending would seriously impair at this time the financial credit of the country.
As I was saying, we have a three-tier pension system in Canada. The bedrock of the system is the old age security program. This is a pension scheme that provides basic benefits to everyone who meets the requirements of age and residence in Canada. In addition, a guaranteed income supplement is made available to OAS pensioners who have relatively little income beyond the basic pension. This benefit is income tested to ensure that the largest benefits go to those with the lowest income, a concept supported by the House in the recent introduction of the child tax credit. In addition, of course, is the spouse's allowance for the spouse of an OAS pensioner who is between 60 and 65 years of age, in order to ensure that low income pensioner couples have an adequate income to meet their basic living needs. Our hope is that hon. members will agree that we will no longer deprive the spouse of this assistance at a time when it is needed most.
The next level of the system is the Canada Pension Plan. The CPP is a compulsory, contributory, and earnings related social insurance program. Thus, rather than being a flat rate universal benefit, the CPP retirement pension is related to the
October 26, 1979

career earnings upon which the CPP contributor and his or her employer have made contributions. Together, the CPP and OAS programs have the effect of providing Canadians over the age of 65 with benefits that guarantee a basic amount of income to all pensioners, and at the same time provide income that is related to their earnings prior to retirement.
As well, the pensioner's income from OAS and CPP is protected through cost of living indexation from the effects of inflation. Thus the first two tiers give the pensioner a solid base of real income on which to build the third tier, which consists of private income sources such as pension plans, investment earnings, and registered retirement savings plans.
In this regard I should touch on another misconception about our national retirement programs in Canada. That is the idea that these benefits should go beyond basic needs and by themselves provide whatever level of security and comfort in retirement might be desired. Such an idea ignores the basic responsibility, and the right of the individual, to make personal provisions for his or her own retirement.
It is one thing for the nation to wish to ensure that everyone has enough to live on. That is a proper and necessary concern for government. But to go beyond that with even the most charitable motives and try to provide completely for every individual through the largesse of the state has far-reaching implications. If we begin to discourage individuals from saving for their own retirement and encourage them to look to the government to provide everything, then we may be destroying initiative and self-reliance. If we allow unions to think that the public programs will look after all retirement needs, then they will quite rightly ignore pension benefits in collective bargaining and concentrate instead on direct pay increases.
This leads directly to another misconception about pensions in Canada, and that is the belief that any and all improvements in the system must come in the public sector. It seems that every time the problems of pensioners arise, the solution that is offered is an increase in old age security or Canada Pension Plan benefits. The suggestion that perhaps there could be improvements in other areas, such as private pensions, is usually brushed aside. With our current severe financial difficulties we must look at all parts of the pension problem to consider the most effective solutions.
Perhaps it is time we realized that not only is it possible to expect improvements in private pensions, but that there may be more room in this area to make improvements than there is for increasing public benefits which result directly in an increased burden on the taxpayer. Private pension plans are widespread and numerous. They are intended, ostensibly at least, to ensure that the employees of both private and public employers can look forward to a secure income when their working career is over.
Enormous amounts are tied up in these funds and the total invested in them is growing at the rate of several billions of dollars annually, yet there is evidence of many problems with these plans which I will outline later.
Pensions
Another area where retirement income can be affected is that of personal savings and encouragement to increase these savings. The growth in registered retirement savings plans in the past few years is testimony to the fact that people will put money aside for retirement if they are given the proper encouragement to do so. Literally billions of dollars are now being placed in these plans every year, and the money invested will in large part be used to improve the future income of retired Canadians.
The success of RRSPs suggests that other areas in the private sector, such as private pensions, could be made more effective in providing Canadians with retirement income. Yet the member opposite seems to have ignored private plans as a source of adequate pensions. The Canadian Labour Congress has in the past advocated that private pensions be replaced by a vastly increased Canada Pension Plan. Instead, perhaps we should be looking at these private plans more deeply to see if they cannot be improved and strengthened.
As I mentioned, certainly it is quite evident that there are problems with the pension industry at the moment. One of the major difficulties is that pensions simply do not cover enough of the Canadian work force. Even though the percentage has been rising the figures published by Statistics Canada at the beginning of 1978 indicate that only about 44 per cent of the labour force is covered by a pension plan. Admittedly, the percentage is considerably higher if we include only the fulltime workers, then about 54 per cent of the full-time labour force was covered. Nevertheless, on a national scale any objective observer would admit that there are too many people without such coverage.
Furthermore, many of those persons who are ostensibly covered by pension plans will not be entitled to benefits. Instead, because they will change jobs at some time in their career, in a large number of cases they will lose the entitlements they have accrued because their pensions are not adequately vested.
Even if they retain the entitlement, they usually will not be able to transfer the credits into a new pension plan. This year the pension industry made a start in providing a mechanism for transfer of pension credits between plans. It is a start that should be encouraged directly by government.
These two major problems of vesting and portability may mean that only the employee who spends a major portion of his working years with a single employer currently stands a good chance of retiring with an adequate private pension. Even then the adequacy of the pension may erode very rapidly because some pension plans make no provision for inflation. The real value, that is, the purchasing power of these benefits will only remain stable if the inflation rate is low.
It is a major objective of this government to lower inflation. However, the high inflation experienced in the recent past has dealt a severe blow to the fixed incomes of these pensioners and has caused many to lose confidence in pension plans in general. The government will encourage post-retirement adjustments against inflation. I hope personally to be able to assist in putting our own plans for the public service and forces
678

October 26, 1979
Pensions
on a sound financial basis, a basis which will serve as a model for pension plans to cope with this problem.
There is another problem as well with survivor benefits. Widows in general are not adequately protected by the private pension system, and often, as is pointed out in studies, they are left in dire straits. We must encourage the rapid growth of survivors' benefits in pension plans.
Clearly, then, there is room for improvements in the area of private pensions, improvements that will eventually affect the incomes of a very large number of Canadian workers and their dependants. The whole area of pension adequacy is one of high priority with this government. As hon. members are aware, it was announced in the Speech from the Throne that we will ask Parliament to establish a committee to review the retirement income needs of Canadians in the 1980s.
Along with the performance of the private sector, there are specific areas of our public pension system that are of grave concern to us; the plight of many old age pensioners, the lack of protection provided for women, the position of the disabled and handicapped, the protection offered to the families of deceased persons, the need for greater flexibility in the age of retirement, and the maintenance of the purchasing power of benefits.
We are all aware that a great deal of research and study has already been done in these areas. We will draw upon the work that has already been done and review it in light of our own priorities. We will add to it what we learn from our consultations with Canadians, with the pension industry, with provincial governments and special interest groups.
An interdepartmental review on pensions that has been going on for the past three years will shortly be available to us. We will as well refer to major provincial studies such as the Quebec Cofirentes Plus study on pensions and the Ontario Royal Commission on pensions. I hope that as a member of this new government I can bring a fresh perspective to the pension area. If our review indicates the need for major overhaul of the pension system, 1 hope we will be free to develop and carry out such an overhaul.
I have one other reservation in reviewing the proposals contained in this motion, and that is in respect of the advisability of lowering the retirement age. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has suggested that OAS and CPP benefits be available to any retired person who is more than 60 years of age. However, it is not certain that the majority of people want to retire at 60, or that society can afford to assist the minority who want to retire early in doing so. This may become even more clear if predictions about the changing age structure of our population prove out.
The time may come when we will have to think in terms of raising the retirement age, or at least of encouraging people who want to continue working to do so. We may find, much to our surprise, that such an idea would be welcomed by many older Canadians and that our entire society would benefit as a result. We will be particularly interested in the findings of the
[Mr. McCrossan.J
Senate Committee on Retirement Age which is now in progress.
There is one other common misconception, Mr. Speaker, which I should mention so that members may give careful consideration to the implications of this motion. That is the view that the Canada Pension Plan is funded through the general revenues of the Government of Canada. Of course this is not the case. The CPP is financed entirely through the contributions of Canadian workers and their employers. Already there are indications these contributions may have to be raised during the life of this Parliament.
Consequently, when we consider lowering the eligible age for CPP benefits to age 60, we must remember that we would be requiring CPP contributors to raise their contributions so that some may receive their retirement benefits five years earlier than others. We know that some workers are forced by ill health to retire before age 65, but I should point out that in many such cases CPP disability benefits may be available. I wonder, however, whether it is fair to ask those contributors who continue to work to age 65 to subsidize those contributors who chose to retire at an early age.
In summary, I recognize the concern of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for the plight of the elderly. However, his solutions are completely impractical financially at this point in time. That is not to say that nothing should be done, however. We will have to change the CPP in the next five years. We must deal with the problems of portability, vesting, survivor's benefits, and protection against inflation in the private sector. We must deal with the problem of a lack of coverage for many employees in the private sector. These problems, the problems of the aged, are real and serious. However, it is my belief that the solution outlined in this motion is not the proper one.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on the motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), which is most welcome in this year of 1979, and especially after the elections of May 22 which brought this government into office, because the election platform they circulated throughout the country had a commitment to lower the pensionable age to 60 for all Canadians.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crom-bie) just tabled legislation, Bill C-6, which will bring very little change to that election promise made last spring by the Progressive Conservative Party. Long before that, my party which was the administration for a number of years amended old age security by lowering the pensionable age from 70 to 65. Of course, deficiencies remained. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made his motion, and the people I meet regularly in my constituency remind me of that deficiency, which is the following: among people between 60 and 65, most
October 26, 1979	_______COMMONS DEBATES
of them, at least the greater majority are women who cannot join the labour force because of their physical condition or cannot find work, and they have no alternative but to ask for welfare, which is not altogether normal.
In his motion the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre proposes that the pension be paid to all Canadians aged 60 and over. This may be going far, as was explained by the hon. member who spoke before me. Monetary factors and the ability of Canadians as a whole to pay should at any rate be considered.
A minor amendment, as I said earlier, is proposed in legislation that will come later, giving the spouse or rather maintaining the spouse's allowance after the husband dies. This means, Mr. Speaker, that in the case, for example, of a woman aged 62 whose husband aged 66 gets pension she is entitled to the spouse's allowance, and when her husband dies the pension will still be coming to her. But what do we do for the other person, the person I was referring to a moment ago, who most of the time is a woman between 60 and 65 who cannot join the labour force? I suggest this is what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should have emphasized in his motion, in order that Bill C-6 be amended to give more help to that group of Canadians of both sexes.
It would have been possible of course in this bill which is soon to become law to phase down the pension; it should be remembered that it was the previous government that brought the pension down from 70 to 65. That government intended to phase down that pension gradually by reducing it year by year, that is down to 64, then 63 and so on until the age of 60. And by the time all those people who are entitled to the guaranteed income supplement get that pension, it is an expenditure, but if you look at it from the other side, it is not a real expenditure because, of course, those who will be retiring at the age of 60 will be making room on the labour market for younger people, people between the ages of 40 and 60, young people coming out of universities and arriving on the labour market now and who really have difficulty in finding a job. People between 40 and 60 regularly have that problem, and when they do not have a job, they have no other choice but to go on unemployment insurance and they are paid unemployment insurance benefits ranging between $100 and $180 a week depending on the salary or the stamps that were paid.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I say that on one hand it is a payment, if you want, that would be made to those people when we ask the government to give that pension at 60 but, on the other hand, it is a saving and I do think that in a country as vast and as beautiful as Canada when the economic climate is doing well, the social climate of course feels the effect-and 1 am not the first one to say that.
Mr. Speaker, there is another point I would also like to deal with. With respect to the motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in anticipation of the bill that will come later, I noticed earlier a release issued by

the Minister of National Health and Welfare which says that all people living alone applying for the annual guaranteed income supplement must have an income below $3,528 for a single person and $5,904 for married couples. Mr. Speaker, today with an income of $3,528 for a person living alone you must figure out the cost of living and think about the various government programs, including the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation which is putting out residential construction programs for retired people with a rent between $225 and $250 a month. If you figure that out, at $225 a month, that makes about $2,700 to $2,800 a year for rent alone. That is one item. Then you must add service costs. And what about food costs considering the increase in the cost of living and all the increases this government is letting go by and that consumers and Canadians have to pay now? Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we should certainly increase this minimum or this maximum of $3,528 for single people and the ceiling of $5,904 for married couples. When a businessman or someone else applies for the guaranteed income supplement, it is unthinkable that they be told that if they have an income of $3,528 they are not entitled to the guaranteed income supplement. I think that this is unfair and unacceptable for Canadians and shows once again the irresponsible attitude taken at the present time by this government towards Canadian men and women.
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened earlier to my colleague, the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), when he spoke of the neglectful attitude of this government as concerns interest rates, the oil price increase, lost business and contracts abroad, the rising unemployment rate, and so on. When the price of oil goes up $1 a barrel, the cost of living index jumps by 5 per cent. Senior citizens and retired people are of course also affected by higher interest rates. They must suffer the consequences of oil price increases. They must suffer the consequences of the borrowing of this government which adds to the debt of each individual Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, this bill. Bill C-6, should be amended. For my part, 1 plan to attend the committee meetings and suggest amendments so that I may represent effectively the people of Saint-Hyacinthe riding. Once again, I am glad to support the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but 1 do not agree with him that basic pensions should be raised to $350 a month for every Canadian man and woman. Mr. Speaker, I believe that this would be going too far. However, it remains that there is a group of Canadians who really need this increase. Others have other sources of income. Of course, every Canadian man or woman is now entitled to the basic pension. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I was happy to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre say earlier that he was not speaking for himself because even though he did not tell us his age, we can see that he does not need any guaranteed income supplement. I am thinking of young people like yourself, Mr. Speaker, like myself and like my colleague for

Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette), who will be very happy when they reach the age of retirement to have a decent pension on which to live.
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying earlier, I visit friendship groups and golden age clubs in my riding almost every week and we meet women between 50 and 55 and maybe more often between 60 and 65; these women cannot consider going back on the labour market. It is unthinkable. It would be irresponsible and disrespectful to ask them to go back on the labour market. These people must be provided for in the bill so that they should be allowed a pension enabling them to live in this country to which they have given their work, their time, their life and their health.
Since they are not entitled to any benefits, Mr. Speaker, we must take action or initiate programs to provide for their needs. Mr. Speaker, that just about covers everything I had to say for now, and 1 hope the government will consider the motion of the member for Winnipeg North Centre and that the backbenchers will convince the Minister of National Health and Welfare that his bill does not go far enough. That is only a small part of the promises and the brain-washing the men and women of Canada were subjected to when they were told during the election campaign that a Progressive Conservative government advocated a pension or intended to amend the law so that every Canadian aged 60 would receive a pension.
They now realize that it is unthinkable since, as we saw today, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) is asking for the authority to borrow an additional amount of $7 billion. Of course, Mr. Speaker, that situation can be blamed on the irresponsibility, the inefficiency of the people across the way. We need only think of all that was lost recently. The hon. member for Papineau mentioned it earlier. Whether it be the Foothills affair, the Candu affair negotiated with the government of Argentina, or even the problems born out of the promise to transfer our embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, we know for a fact that many Canadian companies are losing contracts in the Middle East; naturally, every time a Canadian industry loses a contract, it means that much less money in the pockets of the taxpayers.

That is not to say that the rest of us are not concerned. 1 am sure the hon. member will agree that we too have concerns for people in this country.
I want to remind the House that as recently as in the last month or so we have seen the government indicate concern for elderly people in the same way as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has. We have initiated not only Bill C-6, which has been before us this week at the same time as this motion, but also we have word in the Speech from the Throne that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) intends to set up a special committee of the House to look into the problems of the disabled. The Prime Minister is indicating in these moves that we are concerned not with taking just an age limit and arbitrarily saying that at that given age we will help people, but rather we will identify people who really need help. That seems appropriate in this age of financial stress that Canada is under right now and so well indicated by the questions raised in the House over the last few days.
One area that particularly intrigues me about the arguments brought forward not only today by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-I have heard them often before so I am almost tempted to say "methinks he doth protest too much"-relates to the means or income testing and the concept of universality that the hon. member has brought to our attention. 1 am not taking issue with those concepts particularly, except that I might suggest there is a little inconsistency in the motion before us today. In the last sentence the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests this:
-and also to provide for the elimination of any means or income test from the Old Age Security Act-
The hon. member thinks he is eliminating income testing, but he has introduced into this motion a new form of income testing, namely, if one is working and earning any income, one does not benefit. I object to that because that is inconsistent. There is another inconsistency in that we have moved away from the concept of income testing. Indeed, all Canadians have pride in their country-
